title: Facade Pattern
oneLiner: Hides a tangle of subsystems behind one simple entry point, without removing access to the details when you need them.

hero.name: Simplifier
hero.catchphrase: One door. Behind it, all the complexity you'll never see.
hero.power: Exposes one clean, simple interface in front of a complicated subsystem of many moving parts.
hero.weakness: Try to route every possible operation through Simplifier and it swells into a god-object that knows too much about everything behind it.
hero.origin: Simplifier stepped in after a checkout flow had to directly call InventoryService, PricingEngine, TaxCalculator, PaymentGateway, and EmailService, in the exact right order, every single time.

story.problem: Checkout code calls five different subsystems directly, in a precise order, with no single place that knows the whole flow. Every new call site risks getting the order wrong.
story.solution: Simplifier introduces `CheckoutFacade.placeOrder()`, which internally calls inventory, pricing, tax, payment, and email in the right order — exposing just one method to the rest of the app.
story.result: Every call site becomes one line: `checkoutFacade.placeOrder(cart)`. The five subsystems still exist and can still be used directly when truly needed, but nobody has to remember the dance.

before: Every call site orchestrates five subsystems manually
Easy to call subsystems in the wrong order
New team members must learn the whole subsystem web to place an order
after: One method call handles the whole checkout flow
Order-of-operations logic lives in exactly one place
New team members can place an order without learning the subsystems

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A checkout function calls five different subsystems, in a specific order that's easy to get wrong.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: The new intern called PaymentGateway before TaxCalculator and charged the wrong amount. This is a landmine.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: Simplifier stands in front of a tangle of five interconnected systems, holding open a single door.
panels.speaker: Simplifier
panels.dialogue: Stop asking every team to learn five subsystems. Give them one door — I'll handle what's behind it.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: CheckoutFacade.placeOrder() internally calls all five subsystems in the correct order.
panels.speaker: Simplifier
panels.dialogue: Call placeOrder(cart). I know the right order so you don't have to memorize it.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: Every call site shrinks to one line. The five subsystems still exist for the checkout team who needs the detail.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: One line, correct every time. The subsystems are still there if we need to go deeper — but almost nobody has to.

useWhen: A subsystem is complex, with several classes that must be called in a particular order or combination.
Most callers only need the 'happy path' — a single simplified entry point covers 90% of use cases.
You want to decouple client code from a subsystem's internals so the subsystem can evolve independently.
avoidWhen: The subsystem is already simple enough that a facade adds no real value.
Every caller genuinely needs fine-grained control over the subsystem — a facade would just get in the way.
You're tempted to route every possible operation through the facade, turning it into a god-object that knows too much.
commonMistakes: Letting the facade grow into a god-object that reimplements every subsystem operation instead of just the common flows.
Hiding the subsystem so completely that power users can't drop down to the details when they genuinely need to.
Putting business logic inside the facade itself instead of just orchestrating calls to the real subsystems.
Confusing Facade (simplifies an already-compatible subsystem) with Adapter (fixes a genuinely incompatible interface).
explanation.realWorldExample: jQuery's simplified DOM API over the verbose native DOM, an SDK's `client.query()` hiding connection pooling/retries/serialization, and a `checkout()` service hiding inventory/payment/shipping subsystems are all Facade.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: So the five subsystems still exist behind you?

conversation.speaker: Simplifier
conversation.message: Absolutely — I don't replace them, I just give most callers a shortcut. The checkout team can still call InventoryService directly if they need fine-grained control.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: When do you become a problem?

conversation.speaker: Simplifier
conversation.message: When I try to expose EVERY possible operation from every subsystem. Then I'm not simplifying anything — I'm just a second, worse copy of five classes glued together.

codeBattle.scenario: Your video-conversion library exposes a decoder, an encoder, a compressor, and a metadata writer — four classes that must be wired together correctly for the common case of 'just convert this MP4 to WebM'.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: Simplifier bundles the four already-compatible classes behind one convertVideo() call for the common case, while still allowing direct access to each class for advanced needs.

quiz.question: What is Facade's primary purpose?
options: Provide one simple entry point in front of a complex subsystem
Make two incompatible interfaces work together
Guarantee an object has exactly one instance
quiz.answer: Provide one simple entry point in front of a complex subsystem
quiz.explanation: Facade's whole job is reducing 'call five things in the right order' to 'call one thing'.

quiz.question: Does using a Facade prevent callers from accessing the subsystem directly?
options: No — the facade is a convenience layer, and direct subsystem access usually remains available for advanced needs
Yes — the subsystem classes should be made private and unreachable once a facade exists
Yes — that's the entire point of the pattern
It depends on whether Singleton is also used
quiz.answer: No — the facade is a convenience layer, and direct subsystem access usually remains available for advanced needs
quiz.explanation: A good facade simplifies the common path without removing the option to go deeper when truly needed.

quiz.question: What's the risk of over-applying Facade?
options: It can grow into a god-object that tries to expose every possible subsystem operation
It always makes the subsystem slower
It removes the need for the subsystem entirely
It requires all subsystem classes to be rewritten
quiz.answer: It can grow into a god-object that tries to expose every possible subsystem operation
quiz.explanation: A facade should cover the common flows — trying to cover everything defeats the simplification.

quiz.question: How does Facade differ from Adapter?
options: Facade simplifies access to an already-compatible subsystem; Adapter fixes a genuine interface incompatibility
Facade can only wrap one class; Adapter can wrap many
They are the same pattern under two names
Adapter is only for UI code, Facade is only for backend code
quiz.answer: Facade simplifies access to an already-compatible subsystem; Adapter fixes a genuine interface incompatibility
quiz.explanation: Facade doesn't fix a mismatch — it reduces complexity for a subsystem that already works, just with too many moving parts to call directly.
